name: Sara Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I work at Greenfield Market, a discount supermarket in a small town called Alderbury. Mornings I'm on checkout three, then Wednesdays and Fridays I also do the bakery counter, slicing loaves and loading the croissant trays. The best part is the early crowd, the bus drivers and the nurses, who know my name. The worst part is the cold floor by the door and the last hour when everyone's cross.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what wears you out most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The juggling, if I'm honest. My partner Dev drives the number 12 bus on a split shift, so Maya and Tom go to my sister's half the week. Then there's the till being a pound out and the manager asking twice. I'm still the new girl at forty-three, since I only started here three years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, the hype dies down and we go on as we are. I'd tell my sister that people get excited about every new gadget. Online I'd probably roll my eyes in a comment and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's not nothing, because Greenfield is always squeezing. They already cut the bakery to three days and brought in two more self-checkouts. Even in a flat world my hours are what they are, and the mortgage doesn't care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, take any Saturday shifts going and ask to be trained on the ordering handheld, since the supervisors seem to get the extra pay. I'd keep using the chatbot for the odd message to the school. And I'd try to save twenty pounds a week even if we skip a few things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. Flat but nervy, like waiting for a bill you know is coming. I'd say fine, not great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Greenfield is always squeezing. What does that look like on an ordinary week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rota comes out late and it's different every week. They say they need flexibility, which means I don't get any. Last month I did two shifts that finished at ten and started again at six, and Dev had to swap his whole run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if they cut your hours again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for Saturday shifts and look at agency work in the warehouse by the bypass. It pays a little more, but it's nights and I couldn't do nights with two kids and Dev on shifts. So I'd go to the union rep first, to be honest.

say: I'd tell my sister the **hype** will die down, because people get excited about every new gadget.
At work I'd say we carry on, but **keep an eye** on the hours.
think: Even when nothing changes, Greenfield keeps **squeezing**, with fewer bakery days and more self-checkouts.
My **hours** and the mortgage stay the same worry either way.
do: Take any **Saturday shifts** going and ask for training on the ordering handheld.
Keep using the chatbot for small jobs like messages to the school.
Save **twenty pounds a week** by skipping a few extras.
feel: **Nervy**, like waiting for a bill you know is coming.
S0.quote: Flat but nervy, like waiting for a bill you know is coming.
fieldNote: Sara sees the **squeeze** as pre-existing, so a flat world still leaves her uneasy.
She uses AI casually and treats it as a **small helper**, not a threat.
The late rota and split shifts show how thin her **family juggling** is.

steps.text: Ask for Saturday shifts and training on the ordering handheld
Skip a few extras to save twenty pounds a week
Use the chatbot for school messages and form filling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it'll hit the office first, but we'll see changes too, like fewer people on customer service and the app doing more. I'd tell the union rep we need to get ahead of it. Online I'd share a post about retraining, because I think that's the real answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, if the planning and ordering go to software, there'll be fewer supervisors, and the till team shrinks next. I've seen the self-checkouts double. Greenfield will say it's about efficiency, and my hours will quietly slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a place on the new handheld training and sign up for the free evening digital course at the library. I'd ask the union what jobs are being created. And I'd ask my sister to take Maya and Tom one more evening so I could go to the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but not hopeless. I'd rather be someone who learned it than someone who waited, but I'd be tired a lot of the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask the union what jobs are being created. What would you hope to hear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something concrete, like the bakery becoming a production line and needing someone who knows it, or the new click-and-collect team. I don't want promises. I want names of jobs and a start date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the day would software take first at Greenfield?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rota and the ordering. The checkout stays human for now, because someone has to deal with the woman whose card is declined. But they'll still want fewer of us doing it.

say: I'd say the **office** goes first but we'll see fewer people on customer service too.
I'd tell the union rep we need to **get ahead** of it.
think: If ordering and rotas go to software, there'll be fewer **supervisors**, and the tills shrink next.
My **hours** would slide quietly while Greenfield talks about efficiency.
do: Join the **handheld training** and a free evening digital course at the library.
Ask the union for **names of new jobs** and start dates.
Ask my sister to take the kids one more **evening a week**.
feel: **Anxious** but not hopeless, and tired from studying after work.
S1.quote: I don't want promises. I want names of jobs and a start date.
fieldNote: Sara's **steady** outlook shows: she wants proof, not promises, before she changes course.
She expects hours to slide quietly, so her anxiety comes from **real exposure** and a thin cushion.
The detail about the declined card shows she values the **human** part of the till.

steps.text: Join the handheld ordering training at Greenfield
Do the free evening digital course at the library
Ask the union for names of new jobs and dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's not all spiral, and ask what the company and the government are doing. I'd put a post up asking my MP for a plan. But honestly two years is so quick that the words feel silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the tills go and the shop floor follows, and I've got no savings. Even with three more years for the robots, the company will cut staff the second it can, and I'd be on the list. Dev's job could go too, since buses can drive themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the union and the council to see what help exists. I'd talk to Dev about what we'd do if the mortgage got tight, maybe renting it out and moving in with his mum. I'd also start learning anything I could with the chatbot, like a basic trade or admin skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Not crying scared, more lying-awake scared, doing sums at three in the morning that never come out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said buses can drive themselves. How would that change things at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If both our jobs go, that's everything. We'd have the mortgage, two kids, and zero. I'd have to tell Maya we can't do the swimming club, and she'd ask why, and I'd have nothing to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big firms who can see it coming and say nothing, and the government for being asleep. I wouldn't blame the machine, I'd blame whoever decided that the people who make the money from it don't have to share any.

say: I'd say let's not all **spiral** and ask what the company and government are doing.
I'd post asking my **MP** for a plan, though two years feels too short.
think: The tills go, then the shop floor, and with **no savings** I'd be on the list.
Dev's **bus job** could go too, so both incomes might vanish.
do: Go straight to the **union and council** to see what help exists.
Talk to Dev about **renting out** the house and moving in with his mum.
Use the chatbot to learn a basic **admin skill** quickly.
feel: **Scared**, the lying-awake kind, doing sums at three in the morning.
S2.quote: If both our jobs go, that's everything. We'd have the mortgage, two kids, and zero.
fieldNote: Sara's alarm comes from **two vulnerable incomes** in one household, not just her own job.
She blames **firms and government** for not sharing the gains, in line with her progressive outlook.
She still reaches for **practical steps** first, which matches her steady adaptability.

steps.text: Go to the union and the council about help
Learn basic admin skills with the chatbot
Rent out the house and move in with Dev's mum
Write to my MP asking for a plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is a fair warning and we should use it. I'd talk to the younger ones about learning something that can't be done by a screen, like care work. Online I'd share anything useful about retraining grants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm forty-eight when robots reach the shop floor, which is old for a fresh start but not too old. If I do things right in the next five years, maybe I could be in a job that needs a person. I'm hopeful and frightened at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year I'd save every spare pound toward a cushion, aiming for a month of bills. I'd start an evening course in health care assistance, since care work needs real people. And I'd ask Dev to look at a driving licence upgrade, so one of us has a back-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than the two-year one, because I can do something. Five years is like seeing a storm on the forecast. You can't stop it but you can find your coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd retrain in care. What draws you to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum had carers at the end, and the good ones were people who stayed an extra ten minutes to talk to her. A machine can't do that and I don't think I'd mind that kind of tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the money be like during the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. I'd have to go part-time or go nights at the shop, and we'd cut the holiday and the takeaways. I'd keep the course cheap, something through the college with a grant.

say: I'd say five years is a **fair warning** and we should use it.
I'd tell younger colleagues to learn something a screen **can't do**, like care work.
think: I'd be forty-eight when robots reach the shop floor, which is old but not **too old**.
do: Save every spare pound toward a **one-month cushion**.
Start an evening course in **health care assistance** through the college.
Ask Dev to get a **driving licence upgrade** as a back-up.
feel: **Better** than the two-year one, because there's something to do, like finding your coat.
S3.quote: Five years is like seeing a storm on the forecast. You can't stop it but you can find your coat.
fieldNote: Sara turns anxiety into a **plan**: care work, grants, and a back-up licence for Dev.
Her mum's carers gave her a **real reason** for choosing care rather than just the safest job.
She admits money will be **tight** during the course and plans to go part-time.

steps.text: Save every spare pound toward one month of bills
Start an evening health care assistant course at the college
Ask Dev to upgrade his driving licence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is plenty and we'd better not waste it. I'd tell the union to start bargaining about training now. Online I'd stay quiet, there's too much shouting already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's the one where I can actually breathe. Maya would be twenty and Tom seventeen, and I'd have a trade by then, with the mortgage hopefully halved. I'd be fifty-three when the robots come, but I'd already be in a different place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start on a care or admin course within two years, and aim to get qualified and out of retail by year five. I'd keep the shifts at Greenfield meanwhile, and put a bit toward the mortgage each month. I'd also teach the kids to use the chatbot properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. There's a slope, not a cliff. I'd still worry about the energy it takes, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Maya and Tom about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That jobs change and that they should learn to do something that needs people, and to be curious. I'd tell them I changed jobs at forty-something and it was scary but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong in the ten-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. If Dev's job goes early or the rates go up, I'd be pulled back into survival mode and the course would be the first thing dropped.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so we **shouldn't waste it**.
I'd tell the union to **start bargaining** about training now.
think: This is the one where I can actually **breathe**, with a trade in hand by fifty-three.
The kids would be twenty and seventeen and the **mortgage** hopefully halved.
do: Start a care or admin **course** within two years.
Aim to be **qualified** and out of retail by year five.
Put a bit toward the **mortgage** every month and teach the kids to use the chatbot.
feel: **Calmer**, a slope rather than a cliff, with some worry about energy.
S4.quote: I'd be fifty-three when the robots come, but I'd already be in a different place.
fieldNote: Sara's mood drops to **uneasy** because ten years gives time and a gentle slope.
She worries that **money shocks** like Dev's job or rates would drag her into survival mode.
She wants to pass on **curiosity** to the kids rather than fear.

steps.text: Start a care or admin course within two years
Pay a bit extra on the mortgage every month
Change from retail to a care job by year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because two incomes could go at once and we've nothing in the bank. What would help is a payment to cover the mortgage for a while, free retraining with a wage, and the union at the table.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. I'd miss the regulars, the bus drivers and nurses who know my name. Even if a machine did the till, it wouldn't know who needs a bit of time.

headlineQuote: Even if a machine did the till, it wouldn't know who needs a bit of time.
portrait: **Sara** is 43, works checkout and bakery at a small-town discount supermarket, with a partner, two kids and a **mortgage**.
She has **under a month** saved, and her partner's bus job is also exposed.
She is open to change once proven, uses AI now and then, and leans on the **union** and public support.
She blames firms and government for not sharing gains, and plans **care-work retraining** when given time.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because both household incomes could vanish with no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **mortgage payment** cushion, free retraining with a wage, and the union at the table.
